course.title: JavaScript Basics
course.description: Small steps. Real JavaScript. Build a coding habit one lesson at a time.

lessons.title: Variables

questions.prompt: Which keyword declares a variable you can reassign later?
questions.explanation: let creates a variable whose value can change. const cannot be reassigned.

questions.prompt: Complete the code to create a variable.
questions.explanation: let declares a new variable.
A const variable cannot be reassigned, so JavaScript throws a TypeError.

questions.prompt: Put the lines in the right order to print 5.
questions.explanation: Variables must be declared before you use them.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: a starts at 1, then becomes 1 + 4 = 5.

lessons.concept: A variable gives a value a name. Use let when you will reassign it and const when you will not.
examples:
let score = 0;
score = score + 5;
const name = "Asha";

lessons.title: Data Types

questions.prompt: Which of these is a string?
questions.explanation: Anything inside quotes is a string, even if it looks like a number.

questions.prompt: What does typeof 3.14 return?
questions.explanation: JavaScript has one number type for both integers and decimals.

questions.prompt: Complete the code with a boolean value.
questions.explanation: Booleans are true or false, without quotes. "true" in quotes would be a string.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: When + meets a string, JavaScript joins them as text: "5" + 3 gives "53".

questions.prompt: Which value means "intentionally empty"?
questions.explanation: null is used to say a variable deliberately has no value.

lessons.concept: Values have types. Numbers calculate, strings store text, and booleans represent true or false. null represents an intentional absence.
examples: console.log(typeof 3.14);

lessons.title: Operators

questions.prompt: What is 10 % 3?
questions.explanation: % gives the remainder. 10 divided by 3 leaves 1.

questions.prompt: What is 2 ** 3?
questions.explanation: ** is the power operator: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

questions.prompt: What does 5 === "5" evaluate to?
questions.explanation: === compares value and type. A number and a string are different types.

questions.prompt: Make total equal 20.
questions.explanation: * multiplies: 4 * 5 = 20.

questions.prompt: Put the lines in order to print the total cost.
questions.explanation: Declare both values first, then use them. This prints 30.

lessons.concept: Operators work with values. * multiplies, % finds a remainder, ** raises a power, and === compares without converting types.
examples: console.log(10 % 3);
console.log(5 === "5");

units.title: Logic
units.description: Make decisions and write reusable functions.

lessons.title: Conditionals

questions.prompt: Which keyword runs code when the if condition is false?
questions.explanation: else runs when the if condition is not true.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: 18 >= 18 is true, so the if block runs.

questions.prompt: Print Pass when score is at least 50.
questions.explanation: >= means greater than or equal to. A single = assigns a value instead of comparing.

questions.prompt: What does true && false evaluate to?
questions.explanation: && (AND) is true only when both sides are true.

questions.prompt: Arrange the lines into a working if statement.
questions.explanation: Declare the variable, open the if, put the action inside, then close the block.

lessons.concept: An if block runs when a condition is true. An else block runs otherwise. Use comparisons to make the decision.

lessons.title: Functions

questions.prompt: Which keyword defines a function?
questions.explanation: JavaScript uses the function keyword (arrow functions come later).

questions.prompt: Make the function give back a value.
questions.explanation: return sends a value back to whoever called the function.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: add(2, 3) returns 2 + 3 = 5.

questions.prompt: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
questions.explanation: Without return, a function gives back undefined.

questions.prompt: Build a function that doubles a number and call it.
questions.explanation: Define the function first, then call it. This prints 8.

questions.prompt: Complete add(a, b) so it returns the sum of its two numbers.
questions.hint: Use return with the + operator and both parameters.
questions.explanation: return a + b sends the sum back to the caller.

questions.prompt: Complete double(n) so it returns the number multiplied by 2.
questions.hint: Multiply n by 2, then return that result.
questions.explanation: Multiplying n by 2 returns twice its original value.

lessons.concept: A function packages reusable instructions. Parameters receive inputs; return sends a result back to the caller.

units.title: Loops & Arrays
units.description: Repeat useful work and organize collections.

lessons.title: For Loops
lessons.concept: A for loop repeats a block. Its header sets a starting value, checks a condition, and updates after each run. i++ adds 1 to i.

questions.prompt: Which loop is a natural choice when you know how many repetitions you want?
questions.explanation: A for loop keeps the start, condition, and update together.

questions.prompt: Make this loop run exactly three times.
questions.explanation: The values 0, 1, and 2 each pass the condition i < 3.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The loop runs three times and adds 1 to count each time.

questions.prompt: Build a for loop that prints 0, then 1.
questions.explanation: Open the loop, put the action inside, then close the block.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The loop adds 1, then 2, then 3, giving a total of 6.

lessons.title: While Loops
lessons.concept: A while loop checks its condition before each run. Update something inside the block so the condition can eventually become false.

questions.prompt: When does a while loop check its condition?
questions.explanation: The condition is checked before every run, including the first.

questions.prompt: Stop when count reaches 3.
questions.explanation: The loop increments count until count < 3 becomes false.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The loop subtracts 1 until lives reaches 0, then stops.

questions.prompt: Build a while loop that prints 1, then 2, then 3.
questions.explanation: Increment before printing, so the first displayed value is 1.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: n becomes 2, 4, 8, then 16. At 16, the condition is false.

lessons.title: Arrays & Indexing
lessons.concept: An array stores an ordered collection inside square brackets. Indexes start at 0. Use array[index] to read or replace an item.

questions.prompt: What index selects the first item in an array?
questions.explanation: JavaScript arrays start counting positions at 0.

questions.prompt: Select toast, the second item.
questions.explanation: The second item has index 1 because indexing begins at 0.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: Index 2 selects the third item, blue.

questions.prompt: Create scores, replace its first item with 5, then print that item.
questions.explanation: Create the array before changing an item, then read its updated value.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: scores[0] is 3, so the second item becomes 3 + 2 = 5.

lessons.title: Push & Pop
lessons.concept: push(value) adds an item to an array’s end. pop() removes and returns the last item. A const array can change its contents.

questions.prompt: Which method adds an item to the end of an array?
questions.explanation: push() adds the supplied value after the existing items.

questions.prompt: Remove the last item and display it.
questions.explanation: pop() removes and returns blue, the last item.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: push() puts dog at the next position, index 1.

questions.prompt: Create a stack with 1, add 2, then remove and print the last item.
questions.explanation: The last item added is 2, so pop() removes and returns 2.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The first pop removes 3. The next pop removes and returns 2.

lessons.title: Array Length
lessons.concept: An array’s length property counts its items. For a nonempty array, its last index is length - 1. Read length without parentheses.

questions.prompt: What does an array’s length property tell you?
questions.explanation: length counts the items in the array.

questions.prompt: Display how many items are in names.
questions.explanation: length is a property, so it does not need parentheses.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: An empty array contains zero items.

questions.prompt: Create three names, find the last index, then display the last name.
questions.explanation: Three items have indexes 0, 1, and 2. length - 1 gives 2.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: push adds one item, then pop removes one. Two items remain.

units.title: Objects & Methods
units.description: Describe things, transform data, and build messages.

lessons.title: Objects
lessons.concept: An object groups named values, called properties. Write property names and values inside curly braces, separated by colons and commas.
examples:
const player = { name: "Asha", score: 10 };
console.log(player.score);

questions.prompt: Which value is an object with a name property?
questions.explanation: Curly braces with a property name and colon create an object here.

questions.prompt: Complete the separator between a property name and its value.
questions.explanation: A colon separates each property name from its value in an object literal.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The score property stores the number 10.

questions.prompt: Build an object with score 7, close it, then display its score.
questions.explanation: Finish creating the object before reading its property.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The two properties hold numbers, so 4 + 3 produces 7.

lessons.title: Property Access
lessons.concept: Read or update an object property with dot notation. Bracket notation accepts a string, including a property name stored in a variable.

questions.prompt: Which expression reads player’s score property?
questions.explanation: Dot notation reads a property by name.

questions.prompt: Read the property whose name is stored in key.
questions.explanation: player[key] uses the value of key, which is the string score.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: Assigning to player.score replaces its previous value with 8.

questions.prompt: Create the player, add a level property, then display that level.
questions.explanation: Assigning a new property name adds that property to the object.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: key selects level, so the update changes level from 2 to 3.

lessons.title: Map
lessons.concept: map() makes a new array by transforming each item. In n => n * 2, n is the current item and n * 2 is the returned result. The original array stays unchanged.

questions.prompt: What does map() return?
options: A new array of transformed items
questions.explanation: map() stores one transformed result for each original item in a new array.

questions.prompt: Use the method that doubles every item into a new array.
questions.explanation: map() applies n => n * 2 to each item.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The first original item is 2. Doubling it produces 4.

questions.prompt: Create the numbers, map each to one more, then display the second result.
questions.explanation: The mapped array is [2, 3], so index 1 holds 3.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The original second item remains 2; the mapped second item is 4. Their sum is 6.

lessons.title: Filter
lessons.concept: filter() creates a new array containing the items that pass a test. In n => n > 2, each item is kept only when n > 2 is true. The original array stays unchanged.

questions.prompt: What does filter() keep in its new array?
questions.explanation: filter() keeps the original items that pass the condition.

questions.prompt: Keep only numbers greater than 2.
questions.explanation: filter() keeps 3 and 4 because those values pass n > 2.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The kept items are 3 and 4, so the first result is 3.

questions.prompt: Create the scores, keep scores at least 5, then display how many passed.
questions.explanation: Only 5 and 8 pass the test, so the new array has two items.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The original has four items. Two even items pass the filter, so 4 - 2 is 2.

lessons.title: Template Literals
lessons.concept: Template literals use backticks. Put an expression inside ${...} to insert its value into the text. Expressions can use variables or calculations.
examples:
const name = "Asha";
console.log(`Hi, ${name}!`);

questions.prompt: Which characters surround a template literal?
questions.explanation: Backticks allow template literals to include expressions with ${...}.

questions.prompt: Insert name into the greeting.
questions.explanation: The expression name is replaced with its value, Asha.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The expression inside ${...} inserts the value 7 into the text.

questions.prompt: Save the name, build the template message, then display it.
questions.explanation: Declare name before evaluating the template, then display the completed message.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The expression is calculated first: 4 + 1 becomes 5 inside the message.

units.title: Complexity & Search
units.description: Bound growth, find values, and maintain shrinking search spaces.

lessons.title: Big O
lessons.concept: Big O describes an upper bound on growth as input size increases. Ignore fixed factors, but count dependent loops carefully: two separate linear scans stay linear; two full nested scans are quadratic. These lessons use the usual RAM model with constant-time arithmetic on small integers. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What does O(n) describe?
options: An upper bound proportional to input size
An algorithm that always beats O(log n)
questions.explanation: Big O measures growth, not exact running time.

questions.prompt: Visit every valid array index exactly once, from first to last.
questions.code: for (let i = 0; i ___ values.length; i++) { /* visit */ }
questions.explanation: The last valid index is length minus one.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Each of three outer iterations performs three inner increments.

questions.prompt: Initialize the empty input and counter, perform the scan, then print 0.
questions.explanation: An empty collection skips the loop and leaves count zero.

questions.prompt: One n-element scan is followed by a separate n-element scan. What is the tight growth bound?
questions.explanation: Adding two linear costs remains linear.

lessons.title: Linear Search
lessons.concept: Linear search inspects elements in order and works without sorting. Return the first matching index, or a sentinel such as -1 when no match exists. Before each step, every earlier element has already been ruled out. Worst-case work grows with the collection size. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Which input can linear search handle directly?
questions.explanation: Linear search needs no ordering assumption.

questions.prompt: Complete the condition that identifies a matching element.
questions.explanation: Equality identifies the target; earlier indices have already been checked.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The first 6 is at zero-based index 2.

questions.prompt: Initialize an empty search with -1, scan for 9, then print the not-found result.
questions.explanation: No element is visited, so the not-found sentinel survives.

questions.prompt: The target is absent from n elements. How many equality checks does this linear search need?
questions.explanation: An absent target requires inspecting every element.

lessons.title: Binary Search
lessons.concept: Binary search repeatedly halves an ordered candidate interval. In an ascending array, compare the middle value and discard the half that cannot contain the target. This lesson uses inclusive bounds [left, right]; moving past mid guarantees progress. Sorting first has its own cost. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What must hold for ordinary binary search on an array?
options: The array is sorted in the comparison order
questions.explanation: Ordering lets one comparison eliminate an entire half.

questions.prompt: With inclusive bounds, keep searching while at least one candidate remains.
questions.explanation: left equal to right still represents one unchecked element.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: After discarding values below 7, the algorithm finds index 3.

questions.prompt: Order the one-candidate boundary check so it prints 0.
questions.explanation: The inclusive loop condition preserves the singleton candidate.

questions.prompt: For one lookup in an unsorted array, what is the cost of comparison-sorting before binary search?
options: Sorting is unnecessary for binary search
questions.explanation: The sorting cost dominates the subsequent logarithmic lookup.

lessons.title: Two Pointers
lessons.concept: For pair sums in an ascending array, start at both ends. A sum below the target means the left value is too small for any remaining partner at or below right; move left forward. A sum above the target moves right backward. Keep left < right to avoid using one element twice. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Which input supports the opposite-end pair-sum technique directly?
questions.explanation: Sorted values justify discarding candidates after each comparison.

questions.prompt: A pair sum is too small. Move the left pointer toward larger values.
questions.explanation: Increasing left raises its value in an ascending array.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The first sum is 9; moving left finds 2 + 8.

questions.prompt: Order the guard that rejects using the sole element twice.
blocks: const found = left < right && a[left] + a[right] === 10;
answer: const found = left < right && a[left] + a[right] === 10;
questions.explanation: Distinct indices require left strictly less than right.

questions.prompt: In an already sorted n-element array, why does the pair-sum scan take O(n) time?
options: Both pointers restart after every comparison
The sum operation sorts the array
Each move shrinks the interval by one
questions.explanation: Each pointer moves in one direction, and the interval only shrinks.

lessons.title: Sliding Window
lessons.concept: A fixed-size sliding window reuses a running aggregate across adjacent subarrays. For a window of k values, subtract the outgoing value and add the incoming value. Initialize from a real window so all-negative inputs work. Require 1 <= k <= n. Variable windows need additional monotonicity assumptions. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What does a fixed-size sliding window avoid?
options: Recomputing every overlapping sum from scratch
questions.explanation: Adjacent windows share all but two values.

questions.prompt: Remove the outgoing value before adding the incoming value.
questions.explanation: Subtracting outgoing preserves exactly the current window sum.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The two-element sums are 3, 6, and 6.

questions.prompt: Order initialization for an all-negative length-two window; print -5.
questions.explanation: Initializing best to zero would invent a nonexistent window.

questions.prompt: Why can the usual shrink-when-sum-exceeds-target window fail when negative values are allowed?
options: Every window must have length one
Removing a negative value can increase the sum
questions.explanation: Negative values break the monotonicity that justifies that shrinking rule.

units.title: Data Structures
units.description: Choose and reason about stacks, queues, links, trees, and key lookup.

lessons.title: Stacks
lessons.concept: A stack removes the newest item first: last in, first out. Push and pop at the same end. This matches nested parentheses, undo history, and explicit DFS worklists. Check for an empty stack before accessing its top. Dynamic-array stacks usually offer amortized constant-time push, not a guarantee for every resizing operation. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Which item does a stack remove first?
questions.explanation: Stacks follow last in, first out.

questions.prompt: Complete the operation that removes the top stack item.
questions.explanation: Pop removes the most recently added stack item.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Removing 3 exposes 2 as the new top.

questions.prompt: Order a safe empty-stack read; print -1 instead of popping.
questions.explanation: The emptiness guard prevents invalid top access.

questions.prompt: While validating parentheses, a closing bracket arrives with an empty stack. What should happen?
options: Reject immediately: it has no opening partner
Push the closing bracket as a valid opener
questions.explanation: A closing bracket cannot match an opening bracket that never appeared.

lessons.title: Queues
lessons.concept: A queue serves the oldest item first: first in, first out. Use a deque, circular buffer, or an array with a moving head index. In JavaScript, repeated Array.shift() may move remaining items, so do not assume it is constant time. A growing head-index array also needs eventual compaction or bounded-buffer management to reclaim consumed storage. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Which item leaves a FIFO queue first?
options: The item with the shortest name
questions.explanation: FIFO preserves arrival order.

questions.prompt: Read the next FIFO item using the intended queue operation.
questions.explanation: Advance the head or remove from the front to preserve FIFO order.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: After removing 4, the oldest remaining item is 7.

questions.prompt: Order a safe empty-queue read that prints -1.
questions.explanation: Check for queued items before accessing the front.

questions.prompt: Why use a head-index queue instead of repeated Array.shift() in JavaScript graph traversal?
options: It avoids repeatedly moving the remaining array elements
It makes every graph traversal O(1)
It eliminates the need for visited state
questions.explanation: A moving head avoids the repeated front-removal cost.

lessons.title: Linked Lists
lessons.concept: A singly linked list stores each value with a link to its successor. To remove a node when its predecessor is known, redirect the predecessor link. Searching for that predecessor can still take linear time. Reversal must save the next link before overwriting it, and every traversal must account for an empty head. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What connects adjacent nodes in a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Each node stores a link to its successor.

questions.prompt: Skip the node after current without losing the remaining chain.
questions.explanation: Linking to the successor’s successor bypasses exactly one node.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Redirecting the first link bypasses the node containing 2.

questions.prompt: Save the next link, then rewire the one node, then print its value. Initialize the node first.
blocks:
const current = { value: 4, next: null };
const previous = null;
answer:
const current = { value: 4, next: null };
const previous = null;
questions.explanation: Saving next first preserves access to the unprocessed chain.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time to find and delete a value in a singly linked list of n nodes?
options: O(1), because every deletion is constant time
O(n), because finding the node may scan the list
questions.explanation: Known-predecessor rewiring is constant time; finding that predecessor may be linear.

lessons.title: Binary Trees
lessons.concept: A binary tree gives each node up to two children. Define height here as the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path, with an empty tree having height zero. A binary search tree adds an ordering invariant, but it is not automatically balanced. Shape determines whether search is logarithmic or linear. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: How many children can a binary-tree node have?
questions.explanation: A binary tree permits zero, one, or two children per node.

questions.prompt: An empty subtree has height zero. Add one for the current node.
questions.explanation: The current node contributes one to the longer child path.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: There are three nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path.

questions.prompt: Order the empty-tree base case before its height is used.
questions.explanation: The null base case stops recursion before any child access.

questions.prompt: Insert sorted distinct keys into an ordinary unbalanced BST. What can happen to search time?
options: It becomes O(1) because keys are sorted
The tree automatically becomes a heap
It becomes O(n) as the tree degenerates into a chain
It stays O(log n) for every insertion order
questions.explanation: A BST ordering invariant alone does not guarantee balanced height.

lessons.title: Hash Maps
lessons.concept: A hash table maps keys to buckets using a hash function. Good distribution and controlled load support expected constant-time basic operations; collisions, resizing, and adversarial inputs prevent a blanket worst-case O(1) claim. JavaScript Map promises average sublinear access rather than a specific implementation. Distinguish a missing key from a stored zero. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What is a collision in a hash table?
options: Two keys must have equal values
Different keys map to the same bucket
questions.explanation: Collisions require a strategy to keep distinct keys distinguishable.

questions.prompt: Treat a missing frequency as zero before adding one.
questions.explanation: A first occurrence must produce a count of one.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The key 2 occurs twice.

questions.prompt: Order a missing-key read that prints zero without raising an error.
questions.explanation: An explicit default handles absence without assuming the key exists.

questions.prompt: A hash table uses linear collision chains. If all n keys share one bucket, how long can lookup take?
options: O(n²) for a single chain scan
O(log n) without changing the chains
questions.explanation: Expected constant-time lookup depends on hash distribution; one long chain can require linear work.

units.title: Algorithms
units.description: Combine sorting, graph traversal, priority structures, and justified greedy choices.

lessons.title: Merge Sort
lessons.concept: Merge sort divides an array, sorts each half, and merges ordered runs. The merge invariant keeps the output sorted while both pointers mark the smallest unused value in each run. Taking the left item on equal keys preserves stability. Standard array merge sort uses O(n log n) time and O(n) auxiliary storage. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Which operation combines merge sort’s recursively sorted halves?
options: Merging the smallest remaining front values
questions.explanation: Comparing the run fronts preserves sorted output.

questions.prompt: To keep equal keys in original order, choose the left run on ties.
questions.explanation: Left-first ties preserve the original order of equal keys.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The merge repeatedly takes the smallest unused run front.

questions.prompt: The right run is empty. Order the remaining-left copy to print 4,8.
questions.explanation: When one run ends, copy the other run’s remaining values.

questions.prompt: There are log₂ n merge levels with O(n) total work per level. What follows?
questions.explanation: Multiply the number of levels by the work per level.

lessons.title: Breadth-First Search
lessons.concept: BFS explores a graph in distance layers using a FIFO queue. Mark a vertex when enqueuing it so cycles do not repeatedly schedule the same vertex. In an unweighted graph, first discovery gives the minimum number of edges from the source. With adjacency lists and efficient queues, time is O(V + E). Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Which worklist makes BFS explore distance layers?
options: An unsorted set with arbitrary removal
questions.explanation: FIFO processes earlier discoveries before the next layer.

questions.prompt: Set an unseen neighbor’s distance when it enters the queue.
questions.explanation: Traversing one unweighted edge adds one to the distance.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Vertex 3 is reached through 1 or 2 in two edges.

questions.prompt: Order discovery of a source with a self-loop: mark it before enqueuing.
blocks:
const graph = [[0]], seen = new Set(), queue = [];
seen.add(0);
answer:
const graph = [[0]], seen = new Set(), queue = [];
seen.add(0);
questions.explanation: Marking on discovery prevents the self-loop from adding the source again.

questions.prompt: Edges have different positive weights. Does ordinary BFS guarantee the smallest total weight?
options: Yes, if the source has two neighbors
Only if vertices are numbered consecutively
No; its layers minimize edge count, not arbitrary weight
questions.explanation: Use an appropriate weighted shortest-path algorithm when edge costs differ.

lessons.title: Depth-First Search
lessons.concept: DFS follows one branch before backtracking. Use recursion or an explicit stack, and mark vertices before exploring their neighbors. Neighbor order determines a particular traversal order. On a graph with cycles, visited state is essential. Deep recursion may exceed the language’s call-stack limits even when the algorithm is correct. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What characterizes depth-first search?
options: Always visit the nearest layer first
Always choose the smallest edge weight
questions.explanation: DFS postpones siblings while it explores the current branch.

questions.prompt: Mark a vertex before recursive calls to prevent cycling back into it.
questions.explanation: Early marking stops back edges from starting duplicate traversals.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: DFS explores 1 and its child 3 before returning to 2.

questions.prompt: Initialize the empty graph and stack, apply the source-exists guard, then print the stack size.
questions.explanation: An empty graph has no source vertex to schedule.

questions.prompt: To detect cycles in a directed graph, why distinguish active recursion-stack vertices from finished vertices?
options: Finished vertices cannot have outgoing edges
An edge to an active vertex proves a directed cycle
Every edge to any visited vertex proves a directed cycle
questions.explanation: An active vertex is an ancestor on the current path; a finished vertex need not be.

lessons.title: Binary Heaps
lessons.concept: A binary min-heap keeps each parent no greater than its children. The root is the minimum, but the entire array is not sorted. Inserting or removing the root usually needs O(log n) repair; peek is O(1). Building a heap bottom-up is O(n). Standard C++ priority_queue is a max-heap unless its comparator is changed. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Which property defines a min-heap?
options: Every child is smaller than its parent
Every parent is no greater than its children
questions.explanation: The local parent-child rule places a minimum at the root.

questions.prompt: For zero-based heap indexing, find the left child of index i.
questions.explanation: Zero-based children are at indices 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The min-heap root contains the smallest inserted value.

questions.prompt: Order a safe read of an empty min-heap; print -1.
questions.explanation: Peek is only valid after confirming the heap has an item.

questions.prompt: Maintain the largest k values in a min-heap while scanning n values, with 1 <= k <= n. What is the standard time bound?
questions.explanation: Each candidate needs at most one logarithmic heap update on at most k entries.

lessons.title: Greedy Algorithms
lessons.concept: Greedy algorithms commit to a locally preferred choice. They need a correctness argument, such as an exchange argument, rather than intuition alone. For maximizing the number of non-overlapping nonempty half-open intervals [start, end), with start < end, choosing earliest finish time is safe. Greedy largest-coin change is not optimal for arbitrary denominations. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What must justify a greedy choice?
options: The choice uses the largest number
The input has fewer than ten elements
A proof that the choice preserves some optimal solution
The choice looks attractive on one example
questions.explanation: A local preference is safe only when a correctness argument supports it.

questions.prompt: Half-open intervals may touch endpoints. Accept the next interval if it starts after or at the previous end.
questions.explanation: Half-open intervals ending and starting at the same point do not overlap.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Earliest-finish selection accepts [1,2) and then [2,4).

questions.prompt: Order a largest-coin greedy trace for coins 4,3,1 and amount 6; it uses three coins.
questions.explanation: Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1; the optimal solution is 3 + 3.

questions.prompt: Coins are 1, 3, and 4; the amount is 6. What defeats largest-coin-first greedy?
questions.explanation: This counterexample shows arbitrary coin systems need a different algorithm.

units.title: Expert DSA
units.description: Reason about DP dependencies, weighted paths, connectivity, and shared prefixes.

lessons.title: Memoization
lessons.concept: Memoization caches results of overlapping subproblems in a top-down recurrence. The cache key must include every input that affects the result. Store results before returning, and distinguish absence from a cached zero. For the recurrence ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), with ways(0)=ways(1)=1, caching reduces repeated work to O(n) states. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What does memoization reuse?
options: The result of a previously solved identical state
Any result with a similar-looking name
questions.explanation: Identical subproblems can share their computed result.

questions.prompt: A zero result is valid. Test cache membership rather than truthiness.
questions.explanation: Membership checks preserve valid cached results such as zero.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The cached recurrence produces 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.

questions.prompt: Order a cache read that recognizes zero as an existing result.
questions.explanation: A cached zero is a computed answer, not a missing state.

questions.prompt: A path-count function depends on both vertex and remaining steps. What must its memoization key include?
options: Neither; one global cached result is enough
questions.explanation: Different remaining budgets at the same vertex can have different answers.

lessons.title: Tabulation & 0/1 Knapsack
lessons.concept: Tabulation fills a DP table in dependency order. In one-dimensional 0/1 knapsack, dp[c] stores the best value within capacity c using processed items. Traverse capacities downward for each item so dp[c-weight] still excludes that item. Forward traversal would allow reusing the same item. These examples use nonnegative values and positive integer weights. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes tabulation from recursive memoization?
options: It fills states iteratively in dependency order
It requires every state to be independent
questions.explanation: Tabulation explicitly schedules state evaluation instead of relying on recursive calls.

questions.prompt: Process capacities downward so each 0/1 item is used at most once.
questions.code: for (let c = capacity; c >= weight; c___) { /* update dp[c] */ }
questions.explanation: Descending capacities prevent reading a state already updated by the current item.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Only one weight-2 item exists, so capacity 4 still yields value 3.

questions.prompt: Order the zero-capacity base case. It must remain 0.
questions.explanation: With positive item weights, zero capacity cannot hold any item.

questions.prompt: Why is O(nW) knapsack DP called pseudo-polynomial when weights and capacity are binary-encoded?
options: All table entries are floating-point numbers
The algorithm cannot return exact values
W can be exponential in the number of bits used to encode it
nW is always exponential in n
questions.explanation: Running time depends on the numeric capacity, not merely its encoded bit length.

lessons.title: Dijkstra’s Algorithm
lessons.concept: Dijkstra solves single-source shortest paths when every edge weight is nonnegative. Finalize the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance, then relax its outgoing edges. Negative edges invalidate the finalization argument. The tiny examples use a dense O(V²) implementation; a suitable indexed binary heap gives O((V + E) log V). Infinity denotes an unreachable vertex. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Which condition supports Dijkstra’s usual finalization proof?
options: The graph must be a tree
questions.explanation: Nonnegative edges prevent a later detour from improving a finalized distance.

questions.prompt: Relax an edge only when the candidate distance improves the current best.
questions.code: if (dist[u] + weight ___ dist[v]) { dist[v] = dist[u] + weight; }
questions.explanation: Relaxation keeps the smallest discovered distance to each vertex.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The path 0 → 2 → 1 costs 1 + 2, improving the direct cost 4.

questions.prompt: Order an unreachable-distance guard so no infinity is mistaken for a finite path.
questions.explanation: An untouched infinite distance means the vertex is unreachable.

questions.prompt: Edges are S→A=2, S→B=5, B→A=-4. Why can finalizing A at 2 fail?
options: There must be a negative cycle
The later path through B has cost 1
Dijkstra requires all edge weights to equal 1
questions.explanation: A negative edge can improve a distance after its vertex was finalized.

lessons.title: Disjoint Sets
lessons.concept: Disjoint-set union maintains components using parent forests. Find follows parent links to a representative; union links representatives, not arbitrary interior nodes. Path compression shortens find paths. Combining compression with union by rank or size gives amortized O(α(n)) operations, not a universal worst-case O(1) guarantee. DSU supports merging connectivity, but ordinary DSU does not support arbitrary edge deletions. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What does find(x) return in a disjoint-set forest?
questions.explanation: Following parent links reaches the component’s representative root.

questions.prompt: Compress a path by storing the representative returned by recursive find.
questions.explanation: The assignment redirects x straight to its representative.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: Full path compression rewrites parent[3] to the root 0.

questions.prompt: Initialize the forest and component count, apply the same-component union guard, then print the unchanged count 1.
blocks:
const rootA = parent[0], rootB = parent[1];
let components = 1;
answer:
const rootA = parent[0], rootB = parent[1];
let components = 1;
questions.explanation: Union changes the component count only when the representatives differ.

questions.prompt: Which combination gives DSU its amortized O(α(n)) operation bound?
options: Path compression plus union by rank or size
Only checking whether indices are equal
Sorting the parent array after each find
questions.explanation: The near-constant amortized bound relies on both forest-balancing and path-compression heuristics.

lessons.title: Tries & Prefix Search
lessons.concept: A trie shares character paths among words with common prefixes. A terminal flag distinguishes a complete word from a mere prefix. Searching a word of length L takes O(L) when each child lookup is constant time, for example a fixed alphabet array; map-backed child lookup depends on the map. Deleting a word must preserve branches and terminal flags needed by other words. Examples use JavaScript.

questions.prompt: What does a trie path naturally represent?
options: A sequence of characters forming a prefix
A sorted list of all stored values
A shortest path through a weighted graph
questions.explanation: Words with common prefixes share their initial character path.

questions.prompt: After following every character, exact-word search must check the terminal flag.
questions.explanation: A path can exist without marking the end of a stored word.

questions.prompt: Trace the code. What is the output?
questions.explanation: The shared prefix ca branches to t and r.

questions.prompt: Order the empty-word insertion: it marks the root terminal.
questions.explanation: An empty word ends at the root without traversing any character.

questions.prompt: A trie contains car and cart. To delete car while preserving cart, what is essential?
options: Delete every node shared by both words
Clear car’s terminal flag but keep the branch to t
questions.explanation: A shared prefix remains necessary for the longer stored word.
